newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey vows to halt Cyprus missile deployment.
newsitem.headline: Turkey vows to halt Cyprus missile deployment.

text.p: Defence Minister Turhan Tayan said on Thursday that Turkey would use all possible means to halt the planned deployment in Cyprus of Russian anti-aircraft missiles.
"We are strongly against these missiles going to the island. We will use all our capabilities to prevent it," Anatolian news agency quoted Tayan as saying.
"They will be used when the time is right in the necessary manner and proportion," the agency quoted him as saying while visiting an aviation factory.

Turkey has accused the Cypriot government of trying to change the balance of forces on the divided island with a deal announced last weekend to buy the Russian S-300 missiles that could neutralise Turkish air superiority.
The Cypriot government says the rockets are defensive.

"Defence minister Tayan gave the example of the U.S. 'blockade' on Cuba when Russia tried to found bases there in the past," Anatolian said in an apparent reference to the Cuban missile crisis in 1962.
"Those who play with fire have to take the responsibilities for their actions," Tayan said.
Cyprus earlier dismissed a warning on Wednesday by Tayan that Turkey could attack the island if it needed to protect the Turkish Cypriot community in the north of the island.
"These threats from Turkey are nothing new," said government spokesman Yiannakis Cassoulides. "We have heard such threats before."

Turkey invaded Cyprus in 1974 in response to a Greek Cypriot coup inspired by the military then ruling Athens. Around 30,000 troops are based in north Cyprus, declared a breakaway Turkish Cypriot state in 1983 and recognised only by Ankara.
The Greek Cypriot administration in the south is internationally recognised as the island's only government.
The United States is to send an envoy to the island at the weekend to try to reduce tensions between Greeks and Turks.

Washington has criticised Cyprus, saying the missile purchase would introduce a destabilising new military element and complicate peace moves. Britain's deputy high commissioner to Cyprus expressed his concern at a meeting with the foreign minister on Thursday, a British spokesman said.
